interview_metadata.name: Donte Hughes
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I grew up in the Phoenix metro area, mostly around Scottsdale and north Phoenix, in a pretty stable middle-class household. My parents were practical people: do your homework, show up on time, save money, don't make excuses. I was never the loudest kid, but I was competitive in a quiet way. I liked math, computers, chess, and games where you could see improvement if you studied the system. In high school I got serious about coding after building a small website for a school club and realizing I liked the mix of logic and design. I went to college in Arizona and earned a bachelor's degree in computer science. During college I had internships and a couple freelance web projects, mostly React and Node, and that confirmed I wanted full-stack work instead of something more abstract. I live in Scottsdale now and work as a web developer. I'm not married and I don't have kids. My life is pretty structured: work, gym, hikes, photography, chess puzzles, mechanical keyboards, and trying to move toward senior engineer and eventually technical lead.

follow_ups.question: When you think back to childhood, what routines or habits from your family still show up in your life now?
follow_ups.response: Planning and budgeting, definitely. My dad would track bills and maintenance stuff on a calendar, and my mom was big on getting prepared the night before. I still make weekly task lists, plan meals when I'm on top of it, and keep a pretty detailed budget spreadsheet.

follow_ups.question: Who were you closest to growing up?
follow_ups.response: Probably my mom day to day, because she was more emotionally available, but my dad and I connected through projects. If something needed fixing, building, or researching, that was our lane.

follow_ups.question: What was the first major step that made you feel like an adult?
follow_ups.response: Getting my first full-time developer job and signing my own lease. It was the first time the whole system was on me: rent, health insurance choices, car expenses, groceries, and actually delivering at work.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads was probably sophomore year of college. I was doing fine in computer science, but I was also taking photography more seriously and briefly wondered if I should switch toward design or media. At the same time, I got a small paid project building a dashboard for a local small business. I spent nights learning React properly, cleaning up API calls, and making the site faster. When the owner actually used it and said it saved them hours every week, that hit me. I realized software could satisfy the same creative side as photography but with clearer career stability. After that I committed to full-stack development, started building a portfolio, and got more intentional about internships.

follow_ups.question: What were the actual options in front of you then?
follow_ups.response: Stay in computer science, shift toward a design or visual media track, or just coast and finish without much direction. The paid project pushed me toward taking software seriously.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone influence that decision?
follow_ups.response: One professor did. He told me I had a good eye for user experience but should keep the engineering foundation because it would give me more leverage.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was conscious. I remember opening a spreadsheet and comparing course requirements, job prospects, income ranges, and what kind of daily work I wanted. That sounds very me, but it helped.

follow_ups.question: What mattered most in the comparison?
follow_ups.response: Stability, skill growth, and having measurable progress. Software checked those boxes.

follow_ups.question: Did the choice feel risky?
follow_ups.response: A little, but less risky than trying to make photography my main income at 20.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: More structured career advising would have helped. I figured a lot out through Reddit, YouTube, professors, and trial and error. A real mentor in industry would have saved time.

follow_ups.question: What kind of help would have been most useful?
follow_ups.response: Someone reviewing my portfolio and explaining what junior dev hiring managers actually look for.

follow_ups.question: Did your school provide enough support?
follow_ups.response: Some, but it was general. The best help came from individual professors, not the system.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I'm not married, I'm not living with a romantic partner, and I don't have children. My parents are still important to me. They live in the Phoenix area, and I usually see them every couple weeks for dinner or to help with some tech thing at their house. My mom and I text a few times a week, usually about normal life stuff, food, family updates, or whether I'm overworking. My dad and I talk less frequently but pretty directly; he'll ask about my job, my car, the market, or hiking gear. I have one younger sister, Maya, who is in her early twenties and still figuring out her career path. We get along well, mostly through memes, Suns games, and occasional coffee meetups.

follow_ups.question: What does a typical visit with your parents look like?
follow_ups.response: Usually Sunday dinner, something grilled or takeout. I might update their router, fix a printer issue, or talk through something with my dad in the garage.

follow_ups.question: Do you rely on family for practical help?
follow_ups.response: Not financially, but emotionally and logistically sometimes. If my car had a problem, my dad would be the first call.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My immediate family is my mom, dad, and younger sister. No spouse or kids. We're close but not constantly in each other's business.

follow_ups.question: Do you have extended family nearby?
follow_ups.response: A couple relatives in Arizona, but we mostly see them on holidays.

follow_ups.question: Are family holidays important to you?
follow_ups.response: Yes, Thanksgiving and Christmas are the main ones.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: I have a small friend group, mostly people from college, work, the gym, and climbing. My closest friend is Marcus, another developer I met in school. We talk about code, startups, Suns games, and sometimes life stuff. I have a couple climbing friends from the Arizona Bouldering Club, especially in winter when I go more often. I'm single right now. I've dated, but I tend to prioritize work goals and personal routines, which is both useful and probably limiting.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see friends in person?
follow_ups.response: Usually once or twice a week, like climbing, gym, coffee, or watching a game.

follow_ups.question: Who would you call in a personal emergency?
follow_ups.response: Marcus first if it was emotional or practical, and my parents if it was bigger.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Scottsdale, around the 85260 area. It's suburban, clean, and car-oriented, with a lot of apartment complexes, offices, gyms, restaurants, and shopping centers. It's not the cheapest place, but it's convenient. I can get to work or coworking spaces, Gold's Gym, grocery stores, and trailheads without too much hassle. The area has a mix of tech workers, families, retirees, and people who are into fitness and outdoor stuff. It fits me because it's quiet enough to focus but still close to things.

follow_ups.question: Where do you go most often nearby?
follow_ups.response: Gym, Sprouts or Costco for groceries, coffee shops when I need a change of scenery, and trailheads around McDowell Sonoran Preserve.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: A little. I know faces and say hi, but I'm not deeply connected with the apartment community.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel safe. I still lock my car and don't leave gear visible, but walking at night from my parking spot to my apartment doesn't worry me much.

follow_ups.question: Have you had any safety issues there?
follow_ups.response: Nothing major. Package theft happens occasionally in the complex.

follow_ups.question: Does safety affect your routine?
follow_ups.response: Not much, except I avoid leaving camera gear in the car.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The upside is convenience, safety, and access to trails and gyms. The downside is rent, summer heat, and needing to drive almost everywhere.

follow_ups.question: What bothers you most about the area?
follow_ups.response: Cost and the summer heat. July and August can feel like a logistics problem.

follow_ups.question: What would make you move?
follow_ups.response: A major job opportunity, buying a place somewhere more affordable, or wanting a more walkable neighborhood.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: I live alone in a one-bedroom apartment. No roommates, no partner, no kids. I like having control over my space, especially because I work from home part of the week and keep my desk setup pretty dialed in. My apartment is organized around work, cooking, gym stuff, and photography gear.

follow_ups.question: What part of living alone works best for you?
follow_ups.response: Quiet and control. I can focus, meal prep, or work late without negotiating with anyone.

follow_ups.question: Does it ever feel isolating?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes after a long remote day. That's when I try to go to the gym or meet a friend.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: No temporary members. It's just me permanently.

follow_ups.question: Any visitors staying now?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Do you expect that to change soon?
follow_ups.response: No, not soon.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: No one regularly stays over. Friends might visit for a game or dinner, but they don't stay.

follow_ups.question: Family ever stays overnight?
follow_ups.response: No, they live nearby.

follow_ups.question: Any pets?
follow_ups.response: No pets.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, no one else usually lives here.

follow_ups.question: So the household count is one?
follow_ups.response: Yes, just one.

follow_ups.question: Any shared custody or similar arrangement?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: Weekdays are structured around work. I usually get up around 6:30 or 7, make coffee with an Aeropress, check Slack and Jira, then start coding around 8:30. Some days I'm remote, some days I go into the office or a coworking setup. After work I lift at Gold's Gym three or four days a week. On lighter evenings I cook salmon, chicken, rice, quinoa, or vegetables. On busy sprint weeks I order delivery. Weekends are for hikes, photography, errands, laundry, mechanical keyboard projects, reading sci-fi, or watching Cardinals or Suns games depending on the season.

follow_ups.question: What does your Saturday usually look like?
follow_ups.response: If weather allows, early hike around 6 or 7, photos during golden hour, then groceries and meal prep later.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to bed?
follow_ups.response: Around 11, but during intense coding stretches it can slip closer to midnight.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I'm a full-stack web developer. I work mainly with React, Vue, Node.js, Python, APIs, databases, tests, and deployment pipelines. My normal schedule is Monday through Friday, roughly 8:30 to 5:30, though tech work flexes depending on sprint deadlines or production issues. We use Agile, so my week includes standups, sprint planning, code reviews, feature work, bug fixes, and writing tests. I don't have a second job right now.

follow_ups.question: What part of the job takes the most time?
follow_ups.response: Feature implementation and debugging integration issues, especially when front end and API assumptions don't match.

follow_ups.question: Do you work from home?
follow_ups.response: Yes, hybrid. Usually two or three days remote.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I keep a personal budget, maintain my car, meal prep when I'm disciplined, and study for career goals. Right now I'm slowly working through AWS Solutions Architect material. I also try to keep my apartment organized because clutter makes it harder for me to focus.

follow_ups.question: How often do you work on certification study?
follow_ups.response: Two or three evenings a week when work isn't too heavy.

follow_ups.question: What household chores do you keep on a schedule?
follow_ups.response: Laundry Sunday, groceries Saturday, cleaning either Friday night or Sunday afternoon.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is being more deliberate about not letting work eat the whole evening. I had a stretch where sprint deadlines made me order food too often and skip workouts. I started blocking gym time on my calendar and prepping at least a few meals on Sundays. I also added morning walks on remote days so I don't just go from bed to desk.

follow_ups.question: What triggered that change?
follow_ups.response: Feeling mentally foggy and noticing my workouts were getting inconsistent.

follow_ups.question: Has it worked?
follow_ups.response: Mostly. If there's a deployment issue, the routine still gets disrupted.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I don't have children, so that doesn't apply to me.

follow_ups.question: Do you have child care responsibilities for relatives?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Do children factor into your near-term plans?
follow_ups.response: Not in the near term.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: My direct experiences have been limited. I've had a couple traffic stops, one for speeding when I was younger and one for a brake light. Both were routine. I haven't had anything like an arrest or a serious legal issue. I do pay attention to broader policing issues, but personally my contact has been pretty minimal.

follow_ups.question: How did those traffic stops feel at the time?
follow_ups.response: Stressful, mostly because I hate feeling like I messed up, but they were short.

follow_ups.question: Did they change your behavior?
follow_ups.response: The speeding ticket did. I got more careful, partly because I didn't want insurance costs going up.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Mostly seeing police at accidents or during traffic enforcement around Scottsdale. Nothing personal beyond traffic stops.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever called police yourself?
follow_ups.response: No, I haven't had to.

follow_ups.question: Any neighborhood policing concerns?
follow_ups.response: Not really in my immediate area.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No arrests for me or immediate family. I know acquaintances from school who had DUI issues, but nobody close.

follow_ups.question: Did those acquaintances' experiences affect you?
follow_ups.response: Mostly as a reminder not to be careless after drinking.

follow_ups.question: Any legal costs in your household?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I vote in presidential and midterm elections, and I'm getting better about local elections. I used to skip some local races because I didn't feel informed enough. Now I try to read a voter guide and at least understand city council, school board, and ballot measures. I usually vote by mail because it's easier to research while filling it out.

follow_ups.question: What motivates you to vote?
follow_ups.response: Policy affects daily life, and I don't like complaining without doing the basic civic task.

follow_ups.question: Do friends or family influence whether you vote?
follow_ups.response: A little. My parents vote regularly, and some friends talk about ballot measures.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I think of myself as a moderate independent who leans slightly Democratic, especially on social issues and climate. I care about competence, evidence, and whether a policy actually works. On economic issues I'm pragmatic: I believe in markets and entrepreneurship, but I also think health care, education, infrastructure, and basic safety nets matter. I don't like performative politics from either side. In Arizona, water, housing costs, public education, tech jobs, and heat are more concrete to me than cable-news arguments. I support criminal justice reform and accountability, but I also think public safety matters. I probably sound centrist, but more socially liberal than conservative.

follow_ups.question: Which issues matter most to you personally?
follow_ups.response: Housing affordability, climate and water in the Southwest, tech and economic opportunity, health care costs, and education.

follow_ups.question: How political are your conversations with friends?
follow_ups.response: Moderate. We'll discuss elections or big issues, but I don't want every hangout to become a debate.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I've become more interested in local policy and less patient with national political theater. Housing costs in Scottsdale and Phoenix made zoning and development feel more real to me. Climate also became less abstract after more brutal summers and seeing how much water issues matter here. I still value individual responsibility, but I think systems and incentives shape people's choices more than I used to admit.

follow_ups.question: What changed your thinking about systems?
follow_ups.response: Working in tech actually. Bad systems produce bad outcomes even when people are trying.

follow_ups.question: Have your family politics shifted with yours?
follow_ups.response: Not exactly. My parents are more moderate-conservative, so we agree on some practical stuff and disagree on national politics.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: They affected me somewhat. I grew up in a mostly white suburban environment, so I had to admit I didn't have much firsthand understanding of what other communities experience with policing or discrimination. The protests and conversations pushed me to read more and listen more carefully. It didn't become my whole identity politically, but it made me more aware of how uneven people's experiences can be.

follow_ups.question: Did you talk about it with family?
follow_ups.response: Yes, a little. Some conversations were productive, some got tense.

follow_ups.question: Did it change any concrete behavior?
follow_ups.response: I started paying more attention to local prosecutor, sheriff, and police accountability races.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the core issues are real: unequal treatment, lack of accountability, and trust gaps between communities and institutions. I also think implementation matters. Slogans don't solve policy details. I tend to look for reforms like body camera policies, better data, civilian oversight, training, and alternatives for mental-health calls. I want accountability without pretending public safety isn't important.

follow_ups.question: Where do you get information on those reforms?
follow_ups.response: Local news, policy explainers, and sometimes longer-form podcasts or articles.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel confident discussing it?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat, but I try to avoid acting like an expert.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I've been thinking about how much race shows up through housing, schools, policing, and wealth, even when people think they're just making individual choices. My own upbringing was comfortable and pretty insulated. I don't feel guilty in a performative way, but I do think it's important to be honest about different starting points. In tech, I also notice who gets access to networks, internships, referrals, and confidence early on.

follow_ups.question: Does this affect how you act at work?
follow_ups.response: I try to be fair in code reviews, share context with junior people, and not mistake confidence for competence.

follow_ups.question: Do you seek out diverse media or voices?
follow_ups.response: Somewhat. I follow a broader mix now than I did in college.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I've talked with friends and family, read more, and changed how I research local elections. I haven't joined protests. I'm more of a quieter, research-and-vote person.

follow_ups.question: Why not protests?
follow_ups.response: It's partly personality. Crowds are not really my thing, and I tend to engage through research.

follow_ups.question: Have you donated to causes?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally small donations, but not on a regular schedule.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My friends are mixed but generally more progressive than my parents. Some posted a lot online, some went to protests, and some stayed quiet. My parents were more skeptical of parts of the movement but open to the idea that bad policing should be addressed. The conversations made me realize people can agree on a problem but disagree hard on language and solutions.

follow_ups.question: Did any relationship become strained?
follow_ups.response: Not permanently, but a couple family conversations got awkward.

follow_ups.question: Who shaped your thinking most?
follow_ups.response: Friends who had more direct experiences and were willing to explain without turning it into a fight.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: Overall I'm healthy. I lift weights regularly, hike, and try to eat high-protein meals. I don't have any major diagnosed chronic conditions. My main issues are occasional back and neck tightness from desk work, sleep getting inconsistent during work crunches, and letting stress push me toward delivery food. I try to manage that with workouts, stretching, hydration, and better planning.

follow_ups.question: How often do you exercise?
follow_ups.response: Usually four to five times a week if you count lifting and hiking.

follow_ups.question: Do you have a primary care doctor?
follow_ups.response: Yes, through my employer insurance network.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Easy is having a gym nearby and liking measurable progress. Hard is screen-heavy work, long sprint deadlines, and Arizona summer heat making outdoor activity harder. Meal prep helps, but if I'm deep in code I can neglect it.

follow_ups.question: What healthy habit sticks best?
follow_ups.response: Strength training, because I can track lifts.

follow_ups.question: What habit breaks first under stress?
follow_ups.response: Cooking. I order tacos, sushi, or Mediterranean delivery.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing huge. I had a mild wrist strain from climbing and keyboard work, and I took it seriously because I need my hands for work. I rested, adjusted my desk setup, and used lighter climbing sessions for a while. I also had some lower back tightness after long coding weeks, but physical therapy exercises and standing-desk breaks helped.

follow_ups.question: Did you seek care for the wrist?
follow_ups.response: I did a clinic visit and got basic guidance, no major treatment.

follow_ups.question: Has it affected work?
follow_ups.response: Only briefly. I became more careful about ergonomics.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Health hasn't seriously interfered with work. The closest is wrist or back discomfort making me take breaks or use voice notes for planning.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed work for health?
follow_ups.response: Only normal sick days, nothing extended.

follow_ups.question: Any child care impact?
follow_ups.response: No children.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: A little. My parents are generally healthy, but my dad has had blood pressure concerns and my mom has had some joint pain. Nothing catastrophic, but it makes me more aware that they're getting older. Sometimes I help them with appointments, insurance portals, or researching doctors.

follow_ups.question: Who handles family medical logistics?
follow_ups.response: My mom mostly, but I help with online systems.

follow_ups.question: Has it changed your relationship with them?
follow_ups.response: A bit. I feel more responsible now than I did a few years ago.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: I have decent employer health insurance, so I haven't had to forgo necessary care. The annoying parts are finding in-network providers, waiting for appointments, and understanding what something will cost. My family is similar: they can access care, but the system is frustrating and opaque.

follow_ups.question: Have costs ever made you delay care?
follow_ups.response: Maybe minor things like waiting on a non-urgent appointment, but not major care.

follow_ups.question: Do you use urgent care?
follow_ups.response: Occasionally, because it's faster for simple issues.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Not really alternative medicine in a formal sense. I stretch, use massage tools, heat, ice, and sometimes my mom recommends teas or supplements. I'm not against complementary stuff, but I want evidence and I wouldn't replace medical care with it.

follow_ups.question: Any supplements?
follow_ups.response: Protein powder, creatine sometimes, vitamin D occasionally.

follow_ups.question: Any chiropractic or acupuncture?
follow_ups.response: No regular use.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: I don't smoke. I drink socially, maybe a beer or cocktail with friends, but not as a main coping mechanism. If I'm stressed, I'm more likely to lift, play a strategy game, solve chess puzzles, or zone out with sci-fi. My less healthy coping is probably late-night food delivery and staying up too late.

follow_ups.question: How often do you drink?
follow_ups.response: A few times a month, usually one or two drinks.

follow_ups.question: Any tobacco or vaping?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: No prescriptions for mood or pain. I use over-the-counter ibuprofen occasionally after a strain or headache. Marijuana is legal here, but I don't use it regularly. I tried an edible socially maybe over a year ago, but it's not part of my routine and I don't like feeling foggy.

follow_ups.question: Any concern about substance use in your circle?
follow_ups.response: Not close circle. Some people drink more than I would, but nothing central to my life.

follow_ups.question: What do you use for pain?
follow_ups.response: Rest, stretching, ice or heat, and ibuprofen if needed.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: I pay through employer insurance premiums and out-of-pocket copays. My parents have their own coverage through work or private plans. We're not struggling to pay medical bills right now, but I definitely keep an emergency fund partly because one medical event can get expensive fast.

follow_ups.question: Do medical costs affect your budget?
follow_ups.response: Only in small ways right now, like copays and prescriptions.

follow_ups.question: Do you track health expenses?
follow_ups.response: Yes, in my monthly budget categories.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I'm generally pro-vaccine. I got COVID vaccines and normal recommended shots. I see it as basic risk management.

follow_ups.question: Any hesitation?
follow_ups.response: Not much. I read about side effects, but I trust the general medical consensus.

follow_ups.question: Does your family agree?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, though some relatives are more skeptical.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: I trust my primary care doctor, CDC guidance, major hospital systems like Mayo Clinic, and peer-reviewed summaries when I can understand them. I don't take medical advice from random social media posts. I may use Reddit to see people's experiences, but not as authority.

follow_ups.question: Do you fact-check health claims?
follow_ups.response: Yes, especially if something sounds too clean or dramatic.

follow_ups.question: Who in your family asks you about medical info?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes my mom asks me to look up whether a source seems credible.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly okay, but stretched at times. I'm ambitious, and I put pressure on myself to move fast: become senior, get certified, build side projects, stay fit, save money. That can turn into a constant optimization mindset. The past year had good moments: stronger work skills, better lifting numbers, some great desert hikes. But I also had periods where I felt mentally tired and socially narrow, like work, gym, sleep, repeat. I'm trying to build in more unstructured time.

follow_ups.question: What does stress feel like for you physically?
follow_ups.response: Tight shoulders, shallow sleep, and checking work messages too often.

follow_ups.question: What helps fastest?
follow_ups.response: A hard workout, a hike, or turning off notifications and reading.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.

I value having enough structure to make progress, but I'm learning that structure should support a life, not replace one. Time outdoors matters to me because it cuts through all the digital noise.

follow_ups.question: Which value do you struggle to live out?
follow_ups.response: Balance. I understand it intellectually but still default to pushing harder.

follow_ups.question: What value did your parents most pass down?
follow_ups.response: Responsibility. Do what you said you would do.

summaries.demographer: Donte Hughes is a 25-year-old U.S.-born white non-Hispanic man living alone in a rented apartment in Scottsdale, Arizona (Q11, Q58, Q87-Q89). He has a bachelor's degree in computer science and works full-time as a salaried full-stack web developer with stable earnings and employer benefits (Q65, Q72, Q76). He has never been married, has no children, and is not cohabiting with a romantic partner, while remaining close to parents and a younger sister in the Phoenix area (Q05, Q84, Q99). His life-course profile is early-career, middle-class, urban-suburban, and oriented toward career mobility and eventual home ownership (Q83, Q108).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Donte is highly planning-oriented and responds strongly to measurable progress, whether in coding, lifting, budgeting, or career certification (Q17, Q32, Q61). He shows low present-bias in finances through automated savings, emergency funds, and avoidance of credit card balances, but experiences temptation around delivery food and hobby gear during work stress (Q56, Q60, Q61). His risk posture is moderate and controlled: he values stable employment and insurance while considering future entrepreneurship only after building runway (Q83, Q108). Peer influence matters selectively through professional mentors, developer friends, and family norms of responsibility rather than broad social pressure (Q02, Q05, Q07).
summaries.political_scientist: Donte identifies as an Independent who leans slightly Democratic, with moderate, pragmatic views and low attachment to party identity (Q24, Q95, Q96). His civic engagement is mainly electoral and informational: he votes in major elections, increasingly researches local races, and pays attention to ballot measures and accountability offices (Q23, Q26). He supports evidence-based governance, criminal justice accountability, climate and water policy, housing affordability, education, and health care access, while expressing skepticism toward performative politics (Q24, Q25, Q27). His institutional trust is conditional: he trusts credible medical and policy sources but prefers verification and implementation details (Q27, Q42).
summaries.psychologist: Donte presents as conscientious, methodical, competitive, and self-regulating, with a strong identity around competence, independence, and growth (Q01, Q43, Q109). His coping style is structured problem-solving through exercise, planning, outdoor resets, and technical or strategic hobbies, though he can become rigid and over-optimized under stress (Q44, Q45, Q50). He maintains close but bounded relationships, relying on a small circle rather than broad emotional disclosure (Q05, Q07, Q49). His motivational architecture is achievement-oriented but increasingly tempered by awareness that balance, spontaneity, and unstructured time are necessary for well-being (Q43, Q108, Q109).
